newsitem.title: KENYA: African ministers put pressure on Burundi junta.
newsitem.headline: African ministers put pressure on Burundi junta.

text.p: African ministers cancelled a peace mission to Burundi on Wednesday because its Tutsi military leader Pierre Buyoya refuses to negotiate with Hutu rebels, a Kenyan minister said.

The cancellation reflects a growing rift between Buyoya's isolated government and regional heads of state demanding a return to constitutional legality in Burundi where ethnic war has killed 150,000 people in three years.

"We have called off the mission following consultations. It is not opportune for us to go ahead with the mission. In the meantime the sanctions will continue," Kenyan Foreign Minister Kalonzo Musyoka said by telephone from the Tanzanian capital.

Regional states imposed a trade and transport embargo on landlocked Burundi on July 31 in response to a coup by the army that ousted president Sylvestre Ntibantunganya, a Hutu, and installed Buyoya of the minority Tutsi tribe, which dominates the military.

At a summit last Saturday regional leaders rejected a suggestion by U.S. Secretary of State Warren Christopher to ease the embargo and gave Burundi one month to enter negotiations with Hutu rebels or face further sanctions.
They also decided to send a ministerial committee to Burundi to review a stated commitment by Buyoya to unconditional talks.
But on Monday Buyoya's prime minister changed tack and said the sanctions had to be lifted before talks could begin.
Musyoka told Reuters that Monday's declaration by the military junta had jeopardised the mission.

"If Buyoya had the slightest respect for international opinion and the regional heads of state, then his government would not have issued the statement rejecting talks," Musyoka said. "The ball is now really in his (Buyoya's) court."
In Bujumbura a spokesman for the presidency expressed surprise at the cancellation, saying Burundi would guarantee the group's security -- a concern raised by Tanzania.
"If they do not come, it won't be for reasons of security because there is security here and we can guarantee their security," Ferdinand Nayabenda told Reuters.
Hutu rebels of Leonard Nyangoma's National Council for the Defence of Democracy (CNDD) said Buyoya's stand was a clear indication he had no intentions to sue for peace.

"We know Buyoya is a trickster. He is not committed to peace in Burundi. He has a programme to expand his army and fight Hutus to the last man but we are ready for him," CNDD Africa spokesman Innocent Nimpagaritse told Reuters in Nairobi.
The ministerial group appointed on Saturday at the summit in the Tanzanian town of Arusha comprised foreign ministers from Kenya, Tanzania, Uganda, Rwanda, Cameroon, Zaire and Zambia.

The latest round of bloodletting in Burundi erupted in 1993 when renegade Tutsi soldiers killed the democratically elected president, a Hutu. Tribal hatred has exploded several times since the Central African country won independence from colonial master Belgium in 1962.
An estimated one million people, mostly Tutsis, died in neighbouring Rwanda in 1994 in a genocidal campaign orchestrated by the Hutu-dominated government in power at the time.
